In our previous work, we have generated a BDNF knock-in mouse containing the BDNF Val66Met polymorphism, which provided a valuable tool to assess the in vivo consequence of BDNFMet polymorphism (Chen et al., 2006). Measuring anxiety-like behavior in mice has been mostly undertaken using a few classic animal models of anxiety such as the elevated plus maze and open field tests (Belzung and Berton, 1997; Ramos and Mormede, 1998). All these procedures are based upon the exposure of subjects to unfamiliar aversive places. Anxiety state is defined as the emotion displayed by an individual when subject confronts a stressful stimulus in novel environment (Belzung and Berton, 1997), which could be influenced by genetic components. When placed in open field and elevated plus maze tests, BDNFMet/Met mice displayed an increase in anxiety- related behaviors. Moreover, BDNFMet/Met mice showed blunt responsiveness to the common antidepressant fluoxetine (Chen et al., 2006). Therefore, it may be of interest to examine whether other approaches could ameliorate anxiety-related behaviors in BDNFMet/Met mice. Music has been well known to elicit emotional changes, including anxiolytic effects in humans (Kemper and Dan- hauer, 2005). There have been some clinical findings indicat- ing that listening to music is useful in reducing anxiety (Chan et al., 2003; Haneishi, 2001; Hanser and Thompson, 1994). It has been shown that antidepressants increase turnover of hippocampal neurons and that BDNF signaling is required for the long-term survival of newborn neurons in mouse hippocampus (Sairanen et al., 2005). We have previously reported that anxiety-related behaviors in the BDNFMet/Met mice were not responsive to the common antidepressant fluoxetine. Therefore, it would be interesting to find an alternative way to ameliorate anxiety- related behaviors in BDNFMet/Met mice. We found that music exposure could decrease anxiety-related behavior in adult BDNFMet/Met mice, suggesting music may provide an effective therapeutic intervention for anxiety disorders in humans with this genetic BDNFMet variant. However, mouse's hearing frequency range is from 1 kHz to 90 kHz, which is higher than that of human (Williams et al., 2008). Consequently, music could sound qualitatively different to mouse than to human. Music is dynamic and has complex sounds, which may be really important for its therapeutic effects. Numerous studies on humans have shown that music, as a therapeutic intervention, is used in various fields in medicine (Peretz and Zatorre, 2005; Purdie et al., 1997; Zatorre, 2003). Recent studies show that music intervention has been evaluated as an appropriate nursing intervention to reduce patients' pain, stress, and anxiety levels in pregnant women (Yang et al., 2009), traumatic brain injury (Thaut et al., 2009), and Alzheimer's disease (Guetin et al., 2009). Relaxing music decreases the level of anxiety in a preoperative setting to a greater extent than orally administrated midazolam (Bring- ngman et al., 2009). However, the physiological and molecular mechanisms of this effect remain unclear. Previous reports demonstrated that music-exposed young adult mice showed increased BDNF level in the hippocampus and hypothalamus, as well as enhanced learning performance in the passive avoidance test (Angelucci et al., 2007a; Angelucci et al., 2007b).
